title: Understanding Databases, Tables, and Schemas
description: Learn the relational model: how databases contain tables, tables have rows and columns, and schemas organize your objects.

data.text: Think of a database as a well-organized filing cabinet. Instead of loose papers in folders, a SQL Server database stores data in *tables* — structured grids much like a spreadsheet, where each row is one record and each column is a field of information.

data.caption: A database contains schemas, which contain tables. Each table has rows (records) and columns (fields).

data.text: A *database* is the top-level container. Inside it, a *schema* is a logical grouping (usually by owner) that holds tables, views, stored procedures, and other objects. Within a schema, a *table* is a two-dimensional structure of rows and columns. Each *row* (also called a *record*) represents one thing you are tracking, and each *column* (also called a *field*) describes one attribute of that thing.

data.title: A customers table
data.content:
Consider a simple table that tracks customers:

| customer_id | first_name | last_name | email | city |
|-------------|------------|-----------|-------|------|
| 1 | Alice | Chen | alice@example.com | Seattle |
| 2 | Bob | Kim | bob@example.com | Portland |
| 3 | Carla | Ruiz | carla@example.com | Austin |

Each row is one customer. Each column is one piece of information about that customer.

data.text: Schemas: more than just a namespace

A schema is like a folder inside a filing cabinet. It groups related objects together and helps avoid naming conflicts. When you reference a table, you can use the fully qualified name: database_name.schema_name.table_name. If you omit the schema, SQL Server defaults to the dbo (database owner) schema.

data.title: Why use schemas?
data.text: In real applications, schemas often map to teams or business domains: 'sales' for sales-related tables, 'hr' for human resources, 'production' for inventory. This keeps objects organized and lets you set permissions at the schema level.
Every SQL Server instance comes with five system databases. These are managed automatically and you should rarely modify their contents:

rows: Records system information: logins, endpoints, linked servers, and metadata about all other databases
Template used as the basis for all new databases — files added here appear in every new database
Used by SQL Server Agent for jobs, alerts, and backup/restore history
Shared workspace for temporary tables, sorts, and work tables
Read-only database holding system objects (hidden from normal queries)

data.title: Don't touch system databases
data.text: Never store your application data in master, model, msdb, or tempdb. Always create your own user databases. Modifying system databases can break your SQL Server instance.
SQL Server exposes its own structure through a set of system views. You can query these to find tables, columns, and their data types.

data.title: List all user tables in the current database
data.code:
SELECT SCHEMA_NAME(schema_id) AS schema_name,
       name AS table_name
FROM   sys.tables
ORDER BY schema_name, table_name;

data.title: Key takeaways
points: A database contains schemas, and schemas contain tables
Tables store data in rows (records) and columns (fields)
Schemas help organize objects and manage permissions
Five system databases exist on every instance — leave them alone
Query sys.tables and related system views to inspect your database structure
